good.who: Zhuangzi · Chuang Tzu, ch. 19 (tr. Herbert Giles, 1889)
good.quote: I practise balancing two balls... When I can balance three balls, I only miss one in ten; and when five, then it is as though I caught the cicadas with my hand.
good.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles (London: Bernard Quaritch, 1889), Chapter XIX 'The Secret of Life' (the hunchback cicada catcher)
good.meaning: He practiced with two balls, then three, then five. Step by small step, a shaky skill became sure.
good.reason:
I downloaded the plain text of Gutenberg #59709 (https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/59709/pg59709.txt) and checked it. The title page reads "London, Bernard Quaritch, 1889", the translator is Herbert A. Giles, and the passage is in CHAPTER XIX, "THE SECRET OF LIFE", at lines 7915-7936. The source reads: "I have a way," replied the hunchback. "In the fifth and sixth moons I practise balancing two balls one on top of the other. [Giles footnote: At the top of his pole.] If they do not fall, I do not miss many cicadas. When I can balance three balls, I only miss one in ten; and when five, then it is as though I caught the cicadas with my hand." Every word after the ellipsis matches exactly. The words before the ellipsis are an exact cut from the first sentence. The ellipsis only removes the "one on top of the other" detail, the footnote and the "do not miss many" line, so the meaning stays honest.

The speaker is the hunchback in Zhuangzi's book, so crediting Zhuangzi is correct. Confucius appears only in the frame story ("When Confucius was on his way to the Ch'u State"). He is not credited, he is not mocked, and no ruler or king appears in the quote. The war and empire lines in the paragraph just before this story are not part of the quote. Nothing in it breaks the safety rules.

The meaning line is 19 words with no em dash. Its facts (two, then three, then five balls) match the text.

The quote is 32 words, which I accept as "about 30". If a strict limit of 30 is wanted, the shortest honest cut that keeps the two, three, five steps is 29 words: "I practise balancing two balls... When I can balance three balls, I only miss one in ten; and when five... as though I caught the cicadas with my hand." Keep Giles's British spelling "practise".

good.who: Yoshida Kenko · Tsurezuregusa §150, c. 1330 (tr. W. N. Porter, 1914)
good.quote: He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect... though he have not the natural talent for it, he will not lag far behind the others.
good.work: The Miscellany of a Japanese Priest (Tsure-zure Gusa), tr. William N. Porter, London: Humphrey Milford, 1914, Section 150 'On Perseverance in Youth', p. 118
good.meaning: Keep practicing next to skilled people, even when stiff and laughed at. Years of care beat careless experts.
good.reason:
I downloaded the archive.org full text (https://archive.org/download/miscellanyofjapa00yosh/miscellanyofjapa00yosh_djvu.txt) and checked it. The quote matches word for word. The source reads: "He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect, and is not ashamed when others laugh and mock at him, will enjoy overcoming such discouragement; and, though he have not the natural talent for it, he will not lag far behind the others." The ellipsis drops only the "not ashamed when others laugh" clause, so the meaning stays honest. The quote is 31 words, which is within "about 30".

The section number, title ("On Perseverance in Youth") and page are correct: the passage sits on p. 118, and the section runs on to p. 119. The archive.org metadata confirms the item: Yoshida Kenko (1282?-1350), tr. William Ninnis Porter, London: H. Milford, 1914. The page URL returns HTTP 200. c. 1330 is the usual date given for Tsurezuregusa. The text is public domain, Kenko is not on the used list, it is not a known misattribution, and nothing in it touches politics, royalty, war or religious conflict.

One fix to the meaning line: it said "Years of care beat lazy talent", but the text contrasts the steady learner with "the expert who grows careless", not with lazy talent. I changed it to "careless experts". The new line is 18 words, has no em dash and uses simple words. I also tidied the work field by adding the publisher and dropping the alternate title. I did not check the side claim in the card's notes about the 1911 Sansom translation, and the card does not depend on it.

Two things I judged acceptable. First, Besant (named only as translator) was a political activist. Second, the meaning line leaves out "dispassion", which is a simplification but not a false claim. The meaning line is 17 words, has no em dash, and uses plain words.

Rule: use only one Gita verse per batch.

good.quote: ...carry a young calf in her arms, and daily continuing to do so as it grew up... when grown to be a great ox, she was still able to bear it.
good.work: Essays, Book I, Chapter XXII "Of custom, and that we should not easily change a law received" (translated by Charles Cotton, edited by W. C. Hazlitt, 1877, public domain; Project Gutenberg eBook #3600)

The quote is word for word under "BOOK THE FIRST", Chapter XXII "Of custom, and that we should not easily change a law received". The full sentence is: "...who first invented the story of a country-woman who, having accustomed herself to play with and carry a young calf in her arms, and daily continuing to do so as it grew up, obtained this by custom, that, when grown to be a great ox, she was still able to bear it." He was also mayor of Bordeaux, but this card is about a woman and a calf, not politics. One fix: Montaigne himself calls this an invented "story", but the old meaning line told it as if it really happened. The new meaning line says "In an old story" and uses "carry" in place of "lift" to match "bear". It is 22 words, has no em dash, and uses simple words. Context note: Montaigne goes on to call custom "a violent and treacherous schoolmistress". The calf story itself still shows strength growing slowly through daily practice, so using it for the weak-to-strong topic is fair. I also changed source_url to the HTML page that has the text, and the base ebook page (gutenberg.org/ebooks/3600) works too.

good.reason:
I downloaded the NPR page and checked it. Both quoted sentences are in the essay word for word: "It takes about 10 years to make a mature dancer." and "The body is shaped, disciplined, honored and in time, trusted." The ellipsis only leaves out "The training is twofold. There is the study and practice of the craft in order to strengthen the muscular structure of the body." That does not change the meaning. So I changed the wording to "began serious dance training at 22 in 1916", which matches the Denishawn start and is 21 words with no em dash. I also shortened the "who" line a little.

Rules check: Graham is not on the already-used list. The quoted words are not about religion or politics. The essay title says "God", but it is respectful and does not mock anything.

good.quote: It took me a while to accept that I was asthmatic... But once I stopped living in denial, I got my asthma under control.
good.work: "Jackie Joyner-Kersee: Living with Asthma", a sidebar quoting her in the asthma feature of NIH MedlinePlus Magazine, Vol. 6 No. 3, Fall 2011, printed p. 9 (page 11 of the PDF), US National Library of Medicine.
good.meaning: She won Olympic gold in 1988 and 1992 with asthma, yet took years to accept it and take her medicine properly.
good.reason: I downloaded the official NIH PDF (32 pages) and pulled the text from printed page 9. The quote matches word for word. The source reads: "It took me a while to accept that I was asthmatic. [It took me a while to even start taking my medication properly, to do the things that the doctor was asking me to do. I just didn't want to believe that I was an asthmatic.] But once I stopped living in denial, I got my asthma under control, and I realized that it is a disease that can be controlled." The ellipsis covers only those two cut sentences, and the quote stops at the comma after "control". Neither cut changes the meaning. The attribution, magazine, issue, year and page all check out. The page also confirms the other facts: she was diagnosed at UCLA in the early 1980s, she competed "despite severe asthma", and she won two golds in 1988 and a gold plus a bronze in 1992. She is alive, the subject is health only, and no content-safety rule is broken. One problem, now fixed: the old meaning line said she "learned to manage it daily and won three Olympic golds, in 1988 and 1992". That puts the order of events backwards. In her own words she was in denial for a long time. Respiratory Therapy magazine ("Asthma All-Stars", respiratory-therapy.com) says she was "slow to accept the finding and even slower to embrace a proper regimen of medications. It took a near-fatal episode in 1993 to change her thinking." EBSCO Research Starters agrees: her "aversion to using medication allowed her asthma to worsen over the years, even forcing her to compete while wearing an allergen-filtering mask in 1993." So she won those golds before she was managing her asthma daily, not after. The new meaning line is 21 words with no em dash. It keeps checkable years (1988, 1992) taken from the source page, and it tells the true order: she won with asthma, then took years to accept it and take her medicine properly. "Properly" is her own word, so it does not overstate what she said.

good.who: Johnny Weissmuller · Swimming the American Crawl, 1930

The meaning line is 20 words, plain, with no em dash and checkable facts (1920, five golds, 1928). The quote is 14 words. good.quote: I would stand with my hands against the classroom wall while Ron played notes on the timpani... Eventually I managed to distinguish the rough pitch of notes...
good.work: "Hearing Essay" by Evelyn Glennie, on her official website (evelyn.co.uk), posted 1 January 2015, © Evelyn Glennie 2015.
good.meaning: Losing her hearing from age 8, Evelyn Glennie learned to feel notes with her body and became a world famous percussion player.
good.reason: I tried to refute this card and could not, so it stands as written. 1) The quote: I downloaded https://www.evelyn.co.uk/hearing-essay/ (HTTP 200) and found the exact text: "I would stand with my hands against the classroom wall while Ron played notes on the timpani (timpani produce a lot of vibrations). Eventually I managed to distinguish the rough pitch of notes by associating where on my body I felt the sound with the sense of perfect pitch I had before losing my hearing." The first ellipsis drops only the bracketed aside. The second cuts the sentence after "notes" but does not change what it means. The card has 27 words, under the limit of about 30. A mirror copy (khleedril.org/deaf-essays/Evelyn-Glennie.html) has the same wording. 2) Who and year: the official page says "Posted 1 January 2015" and "© Evelyn Glennie, 2015", so "Hearing Essay, 2015" matches the source. One web search summary says the essay first came out in 1993. I could not confirm that, but the essay may be older than its 2015 web date. 3) Age 8: her own office's FAQ PDF (https://www.evelyn.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/Evelyn-Glennie-Deaf-and-Music-Questions.pdf) says "I started going deaf at the age of 8 due to nerve deterioration." Wikipedia says the same. "Learned to feel notes with her body" is backed by the essay itself. "World famous percussion player" is backed by her Grammys (1989, 2014) and the Polar Music Prize (2015). 4) Rules: the meaning line is exactly 22 words, has no em dash, has a checkable number (8), and uses plain words ("percussion" is the hardest one, and it is accurate). Nothing in the card touches politics, war, crime, disaster or religion. She holds royal honours (OBE, Dame), but the card does not mention them, and the caption must not either. She is not on the already-used list. The essay is under copyright, not public domain, but the rule only prefers public domain, and this is a short, credited quote from her own official site. Caution for the post: in this essay she asks that her deafness not be the headline, and she rejects being called "some freak or miracle of nature". So frame the post around patient practice and feeling sound through the body. Never call her a "miracle" and never say she "overcame deafness".
